reference_title: EM 1110-2-2107, Design of Hydraulic Steel Structures (USACE, dated 1 August 2022)

sections.title: Design Basis
sections.summary: The basic LRFD safety check (Eq 4.1), the HSS-specific performance factor alpha (1.0, except 0.90 for certain structures -- the printed page gives no enumerated list, a source-document gap), corrosion allowance guidance, and the four limit states (strength, serviceability, fatigue, fracture) restated for Chapter 4's design context.
sections.body: All HSS members and connections must satisfy Equation 4.1 for each limit state, unless otherwise specified: sum(gamma_i * Qni) <= alpha*phi*Rn, where gamma_i are load factors, Qni are nominal load effects, alpha is the performance factor, phi is the AISC resistance factor (except 0.7 for forged/cast materials), and Rn is nominal resistance per AISC. For LRFD of HSS, AISC resistance factors are multiplied by a performance factor alpha, applied to account for uncertainty due to lesser inspection ability or more corrosive environments (even so, corrosion must still be accounted for separately). Alpha is 1.0 except for certain structures where alpha must be 0.90. Load and resistance factors in this manual do not account for significant section loss due to corrosion -- this must be accounted for in the design; alpha accounts only for minor section loss in structures difficult to maintain or in very corrosive environments, assuming eventual servicing/inspection. Where routine painting before significant section loss is unlikely, a cross section accounting for anticipated loss must be used. Structures must have design strengths at all sections at least equal to the required strengths from all factored-load combinations (Strength Limit State). The Serviceability Limit State requires checking the overall structure and individual members/connections for operational limits on stress, deformation, and cracking. The Fatigue Limit State is satisfied via fatigue-resistant details and stress-range limits per AISC/AASHTO for the projected loading cycles (Chapter 5). The Fracture Limit State is satisfied per Chapter 5, with additional requirements on Fracture Critical Members per Chapters 4, 5, and 8.
key_points: Eq 4.1: sum(gamma_i*Qni) <= alpha*phi*Rn (loads.required_strength_check)
alpha = 1.0 default, 0.90 for unlisted structures -- NO enumerated list is printed on this page (source gap, see loads.performance_factor docstring)
phi = AISC resistance factor, except 0.7 for forged/cast materials
Performance factor does NOT substitute for a real corrosion allowance
sections.applicability: The fundamental LRFD check every HSS member/connection must pass; establishes alpha and phi before any load combination is assembled.

sections.title: Loads
sections.summary: Defines the full HSS load inventory: dead (D), gravity/mud-ice (G), hydraulic loads (hydrostatic Hs, hydrodynamic Hd incl. flow-induced vibration and overtopping, wave Hw), self-straining (T), wind (W), impact (IM, BI), thermally expanding ice (IX, 5,000 lb/ft), friction (F), live load (L, min 100 psf), and operating/machinery loads (Q).
sections.body: Dead load includes the total weight of an HSS and its permanent attachments/equipment (nominal cross-section, fasteners, welds, coating system by specified thickness); dead load is a usual load. Gravity loads consist of mud (including silt), debris, and atmospheric ice, all highly site dependent; mud (M) is based on site conditions/past experience except a minimum 1-in. layer must be assumed wherever silt can accumulate; atmospheric ice per ASCE 7-22, other ice gravity loads (spray/seal leakage/overwash) from site conditions; gravity loads are permanent loads. Hydraulic loads consist of loads due to water: weight of water, wave action, and flowing-water effects (flow-induced vibration, constricted flow, water hammer). Hydrostatic load is differential hydrostatic pressure (lateral forces, water weight, uplift); it may act as permanent, temporary, or combined depending on structure geometry/hydrology/operations, but is treated as temporary for load-case combinations even if the water level is mostly constant; the maximum hydrostatic load is not always at the largest possible differential head and should be determined with the project's hydraulic engineers. Hydrodynamic (dynamic) loads arise from vessel thrust, downdrag, inertial resistance, overtopping impingement, and hydraulic shock (water hammer); flow-induced vibration is typically not designed for directly (strength/fatigue) but controlled via seal detailing and gate-operation selection. Overtopping must be considered where it may occur (design or high-pool events), including impingement forces. Wave loads (Hw) must be considered where significant wind/fetch exist, added to the hydrostatic load from the corresponding water elevation, computed per EM 1110-2-1100. Self-straining loads (T) arise from thermal/moisture/creep/differential-settlement effects per ASCE 7-22; usually insignificant for unrestrained HSS but relevant for miter-gate anchorage prying from uneven support. Wind loads (W) follow ASCE 7-22 (Category IV criteria for critical structures where wind failure meets critical-structure consequences, else Category II; serviceability uses ASCE 7-22 serviceability wind loads). Impact loads (IM, BI): floating debris/ice impact (IM) applied at/above the water elevation for maximum member effects, from probable-debris/past-experience assessment; see EM 1110-2-1612 for detailed ice-force methods. Thermally expanding ice (IX) is a temporary, extreme-category load of 5,000 lb/ft applied at or within 1 ft below the water elevation. Earthquake (EQ) is covered in section 4.4. Friction (F) develops at trunnions/pintles/pins and seals during gate movement; a load factor accounts for friction-coefficient uncertainty; nominal coefficients are in Chapters 9-16. Live load (L) is vertical load from personnel/equipment/vehicles/storage on operating surfaces/walkways, minimum 100 psf, factored per ASCE 7-22. Operating/machinery loads (Q): under normal conditions, operating-equipment forces are reactions from dead/gravity/friction/other resisting loads; some equipment (hydraulic cylinders) can apply direct loads to an already-closed gate (companion loads to other principal loads); unusual conditions arise from abnormal operation (unbalanced hoists/operation) for multi-mechanism gates, where dead/gravity/friction are applied with only one operator moving the gate and the resulting operator force is a reaction.
key_points: Mud minimum 1 in. layer wherever silt can accumulate (paragraph 4.2.2.1)
Hydrostatic load is treated as TEMPORARY for load combinations even if nearly constant
Thermally expanding ice IX = 5,000 lb/ft, extreme category, applied at/within 1 ft below water elevation
Live load minimum 100 psf on operating surfaces/walkways
Operating equipment (Q) forces are normally REACTIONS, not applied loads -- except direct machinery loads on an already-closed/jammed gate
sections.applicability: The load inventory every HSS load combination (Eq 4.2 and Chapters 9-16's specific combinations) draws its terms from.

sections.title: Load Factors and Load Combinations
sections.summary: The general LRFD load-combination equation (Eq 4.2), permanent load factors (D, G), the generic principal-load-factor conditions (1.2/1.3/1.4/1.5 by return-period predictability), specific principal factors for L/T/W/BI, companion load factors (F/L/T/W/other), and the consolidated Table 4.1.
sections.body: Design equations for individual HSS are provided in Chapters 9-16; the general equation for combining loads for the strength limit state is Eq 4.2: U = sum(gamma_p*Lp) + gamma_pr*Lpr + sum(gamma_c*Ltc) + gamma_c*Ldc, where Lpr (the principal load) is normally extreme but may be unusual or usual if the maximum load meets those category definitions. Permanent loads (D, G) use maximum/minimum factors applied for greatest effect: D combined with other loads gamma_p=1.2 or 0.9, D used alone as a principal load gamma_pr=1.4, G gamma_p=1.6 or 0. Principal load factors provide low probability of failure; except where a Table 4.1/Chapter 9-16 value applies, generic conditions are: Condition 1 (maximum loading not limited by geometry, return period estimable, e.g. wind/most wave loads; minimum design return periods >= 3,000 years normal / 10,000 years critical) gamma_pr=1.2; Condition 2 (maximum loading limited by geometry/physical factors, return period calculable/estimable) banded by the resulting return-period range -- extreme range (< 3,000/10,000 yr but > 300/750 yr) gamma_pr=1.3, unusual range (< 300/750 yr but > 10 yr) gamma_pr=1.4, usual range (< 10 yr) gamma_pr=1.5; Condition 3 (return period unknown, treated as very-low-probability extreme, e.g. impact/thermal ice/barge impact/many hydrodynamic loads) gamma_pr=1.3. Specific principal factors: L gamma_pr=1.6; T gamma_pr=1.2 (min); W gamma_pr=1.0; BI gamma_pr=1.3. Companion load factors (gamma_c) depend on load source: live/self-straining/wind companion factors come from ASCE 7-22 combinations; friction gamma_c=1.4 (since nominal Chapters 9-16 friction values represent above-expected-but-sub-ultimate conditions); all other temporary/dynamic companion loads (minimum 10-year return period per 3.3.3.3, or per 4.2.7 for earthquake) gamma_c=1.0. Specific companion factors: F gamma_c=1.4; L gamma_c=1.0 (ASCE 7-22); T gamma_c=1.0 (ASCE 7-22); W gamma_c=0.5 (ASCE 7-22); all other Lt/Ld gamma_c=1.0. Table 4.1 consolidates all of the above (see fatigue load factors, section 5.1).
key_points: Eq 4.2: U = sum(gamma_p*Lp) + gamma_pr*Lpr + sum(gamma_c*Ltc) + gamma_c*Ldc (loads.load_combination_lrfd)
D: gamma_p=1.2/0.9 combined, 1.4 alone; G: gamma_p=1.6/0
Generic principal conditions 1/2/3 = 1.2 / 1.3-1.5 (banded) / 1.3 (loads.principal_load_condition_factor)
Specific principal factors: L=1.6, T=1.2(min), W=1.0, BI=1.3
Companion factors: F=1.4, L/T=1.0 (ASCE 7-22), W=0.5 (ASCE 7-22), other=1.0
Table 4.1 (loads.TABLE_4_1_PERMANENT / TABLE_4_1_TEMPORARY_DYNAMIC) consolidates the full set
sections.applicability: The central load-factor selection logic used to assemble every strength-limit-state load combination in this manual.

sections.title: Earthquake
sections.summary: Introduces the two design earthquakes (OBE=unusual, MDE=extreme, MDE=MCE for critical features per ER 1110-2-1806); simplified screening vs. response-spectrum/time-history methods; ground-motion sourcing (USGS maps/tools, or site-specific studies where seismicity/consequence warrant); the Westergaard hydrodynamic pressure approximation (Eq 4.3) combined with the HSS-support acceleration amplification (Eq 4.4-4.6, Table 4.2 -- see seismic_amplification.py); and the three earthquake load combinations (Eq 4.7/4.8/4.9).
sections.body: Two earthquakes are considered per ER 1110-2-1806: the Operating Basis Earthquake (OBE, an unusual load) and the Maximum Design Earthquake (MDE, an extreme load; equals the Maximum Credible Earthquake (MCE) for critical features). Earthquake loads are low-probability, short-duration principal loads combined with companion loads (typically Dead, Gravity, and Hydrostatic) per paragraph 4.4.7. The simplified screening method may be used when earthquake is not the controlling load case; final design when earthquake controls must use response-spectrum or time-history methods. Absent project-specific ground motions, OBE/MDE may come from USGS spectral acceleration maps/web tools (adjusted from site class B/C via ASCE 7-22 factors if needed); per ER 1110-2-1806, site-specific studies are required in regions of high-to-moderate seismicity where earthquake loading controls the design, developing response spectra (EM 1110-2-6050) and/or time histories (EM 1110-2-6051). In addition to the HSS's own inertia, water above/adjacent to/surrounding the structure increases inertial forces via hydrodynamic pressure from the displaced structure moving the surrounding water; for simplified screening this is approximated by the Westergaard (1933) method, Eq 4.3: p = gamma_w*ac*sqrt(H*y). The maximum acceleration at the HSS support (ac) may differ from the maximum ground acceleration depending on structure height, per Eq 4.4 (with a stated but, per the worked Appendix D example, apparently-unused 'Pseudo Static Correction Factor' C=0.75 -- see seismic_amplification.py docstring), using the spectral acceleration SA(T1,zeta), a geometry/mode-shape-derived scale factor Gamma-tilde, and the normalized mode shape phi(z); Table 4.2 gives Gamma-tilde by dam height-to-width ratio (>1h:1.5w -> 2.8; 1h:1.5w to 1h:3w -> 1.5; <1h:3w -> use PGA directly), and Eq 4.5/4.6 give the closed-form mode shape and full ac equation (identical to Appendix D's Eq D.9/D.8, which includes a fully worked validation example). Earthquake load combination equations (variable names as previously defined; hydrostatic load per 4.2.3.1): Eq 4.7 U = sum(gamma_p*Lp) + 1.5*EQ + gamma_c*Ltc (standard OBE ground motion); Eq 4.8 U = sum(gamma_p*Lp) + 1.25*EQ + gamma_c*Ltc (standard MDE ground motion); Eq 4.9 U = sum(gamma_p*Lp) + 1.0*EQ + 1.0*Lt (site-specific MDE/MCE ground motion, unfactored since the site-specific analysis already reflects the target reliability).
key_points: OBE = unusual load; MDE = extreme load (= MCE for critical features)
Site-specific ground-motion studies required in high/moderate seismicity where EQ controls (per ER 1110-2-1806)
Westergaard pressure Eq 4.3: p = gamma_w*ac*sqrt(H*y) (seismic_amplification.westergaard_pressure)

ac amplification via Table 4.2 (height/width -> Gamma-tilde) + mode shape phi(z), Eq 4.4-4.6 (see seismic_amplification.py for the validated Eq 4.6/D.8 form and the C-factor/Table-4.2-citation discrepancies)
Eq 4.7/4.8/4.9: standard-OBE (1.5EQ) / standard-MDE (1.25EQ) / site-specific (1.0EQ) load combinations (loads.earthquake_load_combination)
sections.applicability: Full seismic design path for HSS mounted on or near a concrete gravity dam, from ground-motion selection through the acceleration amplification to the final factored load combination.
